# The AI-Native Design Life Cycle {#sec-architecture-20-ontology}

::: {.epigraph}
> "All models are wrong but some are useful."
>
> — George E. P. Box, *Robustness in the Strategy of Scientific Model Building* [@Box1979Robustness, p. 202]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *Once an AI-native design system is being considered, how should the design work be organized, and why does that structure matter?*

**Core thesis:** *An explicit life cycle connects architectural intent to a reviewed decision. This chapter organizes its responsibilities into six stages (Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit), linked by structured execution records.*
:::

A generator can propose a new accumulator organization in seconds. The proposal helps only if the surrounding system can compile it, simulate it, check it physically, and trace a failure back to the assumption it tests, without losing track of which candidate produced which result. This chapter organizes that work into an explicit six-stage life cycle: Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit (@fig-ch03-cover-map). Each stage answers a distinct engineering obligation, from bounding the physical design space to establishing what returned metrics justify doing next.

Each stage boundary exposes what was assumed, what ran, and what was learned, which makes it easier to see which assumption a failure calls into question before it propagates across abstraction seams. Through a constructed walkthrough of a neural processing unit (NPU) accumulator block in the prospective Lighthouse system-on-chip (SoC), this chapter illustrates how structured execution records can preserve the lineage from architectural intent to physical signoff, so that a surprising tool result can be traced back to the assumption it tests.

![**Six life-cycle responsibilities establish inspectable handoffs.** The design process progresses through Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit. Targeted feedback routes unexpected outcomes or inadequate evidence back to the specific prior responsibility that owns the shortfall, maintaining explicit provenance across human and automated contributions.](images/ch03-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch03-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which six life-cycle activities run from formulation through review and decision. Feedback returns work to earlier activities for investigation and revision."}

## The Six Stages of the AI-Native Life Cycle {#sec-arch2-ontology}

The pressures in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales affect the whole path from a design idea to an engineering decision. Generating alternatives more quickly helps only if the team can implement them, compare them under meaningful conditions, and use the results to decide what to try next. The life cycle connects those activities so that progress in one can inform the others.

Separating requirements, design alternatives, implementation, and verification has deep precedents in systems engineering, where these activities remain iterative and interdependent [@NASA2017SystemsEngineeringHandbook, chap. 4]. Rather than prescribing six separate teams, six software components, or six rigid steps in a tool flow, the six stages used here organize recurring architecture work so a reader can follow a design, see what its measurements establish, and identify what needs revision. Because each stage names a distinct engineering obligation and the assumptions or artifacts it owns, a later review in Commit can reopen Formulate directly without restarting valid intermediate work.

Consider a candidate that misses its clock-frequency target: because the failure might stem from an unrealistic target, a microarchitectural bottleneck, or misconfigured analysis constraints, each explanation calls for a different repair. While stage boundaries do not diagnose the failure by themselves, they separate those possibilities cleanly, and existing milestones such as register-transfer level (RTL) freeze and timing signoff remain in place while the six stages describe work that recurs before and between them.

Catching problems early matters because diagnostic cost rises steeply down the stack. Whereas a lint or synthesis error points directly to the offending line, a setup violation found at timing signoff arrives as a failing path through a gate-level netlist, evaluated with extracted resistance and capacitance across several process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners far from the architectural choice that produced it. Because tracing that path back to an upstream pipeline decision takes far more engineering work and tool runs than rejecting the decision during Formulate or Explore, any exploration method that generates RTL freely while deferring checks to late-stage physical signoff inherits that diagnostic burden for every candidate it sends forward.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Isolate failure domains for repair"}
**The principle:** Separate design activities so that a failed result can be traced to the assumptions, artifacts, or checks that need revision.

**The application:** Use the available diagnostics to choose what to revisit, preserving earlier work whose assumptions still hold. When the cause is uncertain or spans several activities, investigate it before choosing a repair.
:::

Each stage answers a question that the next activity depends on. The sequence provides an initial reading order; feedback can send work back to any earlier stage.

1. **Formulate.** What should the design achieve? State the question, baseline, constraints, permitted changes, and checks that will judge the result.
2. **Explore.** What alternatives are worth testing? Generate or select candidates, including different hardware and software organizations when the question permits them.
3. **Implement.** How can each candidate be tested? Develop the required models, RTL, and software, and run the tools needed to examine them.
4. **Evaluate.** What do the results establish? Check that the observations are valid for the intended comparison, then determine which requirements are satisfied or still unresolved.
5. **Interpret.** Why did the design behave this way? Test explanations for gains and failures, and use what is learned to guide further design work.
6. **Commit.** What should happen next? Review the study and decide whether to advance a candidate, reject it, revise the study, or stop.

The operational layers defined in @sec-three-operational-layers determine which repairs may run automatically across these stages. Whereas a Layer 1 workflow uses a model to draft an isolated block during Implement or inspect a timing report during Interpret while engineers coordinate integration, clock-domain crossing (CDC) checks, and repair, a Layer 2 workflow fixes a structural container $\Theta$ in Formulate so an optimizer can search parameters $\theta \in \Theta$ across Explore, Implement, and Evaluate, handing the question back to the architect whenever a repair would alter a frozen interface or topology. A Layer 3 system would be permitted to carry physical feedback back into Explore and Implement to revise hardware organization and software together, although whether that broader cross-layer capability (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect) can operate reliably and at lower total cost than a conventional team remains open.

Prediction, generation, and optimization are methods deployed within the workflow rather than separate stages, because each can contribute across all three layers.

Suppose one candidate Lighthouse design uses an NPU for part of its extended reality (XR) workload, one of the compute options left open in @sec-moonshot. Focusing on the accumulator block that combines partial products into matrix-multiplication results, this walkthrough asks how to improve throughput within the block's allocated timing and power limits in a 3\ nm-class design flow. Although the candidates, timing failure, and diagnosis are constructed teaching examples, following a single block through all six stages shows how their responsibilities and feedback paths connect (@fig-ontology-loop).

![**The six-stage design life cycle carries system intent to a reviewed decision.** Execution advances systematically through Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit. Targeted repair routes unexpected outcomes back to re-evaluate the responsible stage, such as reopening formulation when targets prove physically unattainable, without restarting valid intermediate progress.](images/fig-ontology-loop){#fig-ontology-loop width="80%" fig-alt="Life-cycle diagram of six stages arranged in two rows, with arrows from Formulate through Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, to Commit. One return arrow leads from the decision back to formulation."}

One application of the life cycle to a bounded architecture question is a *scoped study*. The NPU block study is one such application; it does not settle every question about the processor that contains it. The sequence runs from initial formulation to reviewed commitment, but its essential property is the return path: when evaluation or interpretation uncovers a constraint violation, targeted feedback routes the failure directly to the responsible stage rather than restarting the entire pipeline. Within the study, a design loop occurs when an empirical result changes the candidate microarchitecture or the plan itself and triggers another action, as defined in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales. Merely completing a predetermined parameter sweep without adaptive feedback is not a design loop.

Studies can also depend on one another across hierarchy levels. A subsystem study sets the NPU block's power and timing allocations within the Lighthouse subsystem's 3\ W envelope, while the block study discovers whether those allocations can sustain a viable accumulator organization. If no legal candidate closes timing, that shortfall routes back to re-evaluate the subsystem contract. The walkthrough traces this block study through all six stages before examining how to coordinate multiple coupled studies.

### Stage 1: Formulating Core Architecture Questions

Formulation turns a broad product goal into a testable comparison against an explicit baseline. For the NPU block, "improve throughput" becomes a question of whether an alternative organization can process more matrix-multiplication results per unit time than the existing accumulator while meeting the target clock period, required numerical behavior, and allocated area and power budgets (which must leave room for the rest of the Lighthouse subsystem within its 3\ W envelope). Making that comparison trustworthy requires characterizing the baseline's assumptions up front: if the reference model treats memory service as instantaneous, an apparent accumulator bottleneck may vanish once realistic contention is included. Formulation therefore specifies the reference design, workload phases, tool assumptions, and verification checks while separating fixed system contracts from choices the study is free to vary.

That boundary between fixed contracts and open choices also defines how far automated repair may reach. In the NPU accumulator walkthrough, the study may modify the internal datapath organization, pipeline structure, and supporting software schedule while holding external bus interfaces and numerical accuracy fixed; if downstream physical checks show that the bus protocol itself throttles throughput, the repair loop cannot alter that protocol unilaterally and must return the question to the architect. Together with an explicit run budget and stopping criteria, these rules yield a testable question and an execution plan against which Explore can propose candidates.

### Stage 2: Exploring Alternatives

Once Formulate establishes the question and permitted changes, exploration develops alternatives worth implementing. While a parameter sweep inside a fixed container can adjust queue depths or clock multipliers around a centralized crossbar using cycle-level simulators or fast analytical surrogates, it cannot alter the crossbar topology itself. Proposing a structural alternative leaves that container: a generator might replace the crossbar with distributed accumulator banks and local reduction trees, because such a change is viable only when paired with the compiler lowering schedule and dataflow orchestration needed to produce correct matrix results on the new organization.

These alternatives trade more than throughput. Additional parallel paths may require more storage and routing, while banking may shorten critical interconnect lines at the cost of bank conflicts or extra reduction stages. Exploration exposes these tradeoffs and selects informative candidates, rather than certifying physical feasibility from a high-level description. A cycle simulator that omits interconnect wire delay[^fn-wire-delay-c03] can overstate the throughput of a wider centralized crossbar because it ignores the physical resistance and capacitance of long wires. Any exploration guided only by such surrogates, at any layer, can propose candidates that look optimal in simulation but fail timing signoff. The protection is a return path from physical evaluation back to exploration, for parameter changes and structural changes alike.

[^fn-wire-delay-c03]: **Interconnect wire delay**: In advanced nanoscale fabrication nodes, wire resistance and parasitic capacitance scale unfavorably compared to transistor gate delays. Depending on wire length and the target clock period, long interconnect wires across wide crossbars may need repeater buffers or pipelined traversal. A model that assumes single-cycle communication can then overestimate the implementation's throughput.

Choosing how to search depends on what limits the study. When only a few accumulator organizations are at issue, implementing and comparing them directly is often cheapest; when the candidate space grows larger, prediction can screen out weak designs, optimization can allocate scarce evaluations, and generation can propose new topologies. Because each method introduces its own setup costs and modeling assumptions, the question is whether it helps answer the architectural comparison within the available budget (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization).

Throughout this search, the exploration history records why each candidate was selected or set aside. Proposals that violate a frozen interface can be rejected immediately, whereas a candidate with uncertain timing may still merit implementation if it tests a useful microarchitectural hypothesis. While changes permitted by the study plan proceed directly to Implement, any proposal that requires altering a system interface or power allocation routes back to Formulate for scope review.

### Stage 3: Implementing Testable Representations

A candidate organization needs a testable implementation before its proposed benefits can be assessed. For the banked NPU alternative, a joint hardware and software implementation would generate transaction-level models of data movement, synthesizable RTL for distributed accumulator banks, and a compiled software schedule that orchestrates matrix tiles across those banks. The team checks these artifacts against a reference fixed before generation, such as formal property assertions or a golden model, for the independence reason given in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales. A banked accumulator is not a valid candidate if its compiled software still assumes the access pattern of a centralized crossbar.

Automated research toolchains such as OpenROAD Flow Scripts demonstrate scriptable logic synthesis, placement, and routing on open nodes [@OpenROADDocs], but 3\ nm-class commercial realization requires proprietary foundry-qualified design rule decks and signoff engines. License availability and tool runtime constrain the affordable rate and concurrency of physical checks. An early behavioral model can test an algorithm or schedule, while a physical timing estimate needs the appropriate implementation and electrical models. Choosing which design relationships to preserve at each level is the representation problem developed in @sec-data-representations-world-models.

Implementation also determines which verification checks to run first. Verification costs rise across abstraction levels, from quick syntax linting and functional simulation to much longer implementation, place-and-route, and timing runs. Teams therefore screen candidates in tiers, rejecting flawed ones with cheap checks before committing expensive physical implementation cycles.

Tiered screening saves compute only when each early check is treated as a filter rather than a certificate: passing a behavioral simulation justifies spending synthesis time on a candidate, but it says nothing about whether the resulting layout will satisfy the foundry's physical design rules.[^fn-drc-c03]

[^fn-drc-c03]: **Design rule check (DRC)**: A check of layout geometry against a semiconductor foundry's manufacturing rules, such as minimum wire widths and spacing. Passing establishes compliance with the rules checked, not guaranteed fabrication yield. Behavioral simulation does not establish compliance with these rules.

Even before physical checks begin, implementation has to verify that the tools actually tested the intended design. A syntactically clean script can still point to the wrong top-level module, hold an active-low reset asserted throughout simulation, or skip the target workload phase; similarly, a generated RTL block can pass its unit testbench while violating an interconnect handshake, omitting power-domain isolation cells,[^fn-power-domain-isolation-c03] or compiling against a mismatched software target. Keeping the candidate, supporting software, interface assertions, and tool inputs linked throughout execution prevents those silent mismatches.

[^fn-power-domain-isolation-c03]: **Power-domain isolation**: Specialized clamp circuits placed at boundaries between independent voltage or power domains on a system-on-chip (SoC). When a block is powered off to eliminate static leakage, isolation cells hold boundary signals at defined logic levels (0 or 1) to prevent floating inputs and destructive short-circuit crowbar currents in neighboring active blocks.

When a tool run fails outright, the harness must also separate operational faults from bad hardware before feeding the outcome back into search. A license checkout timeout says nothing about circuit timing, and a host out-of-memory kill might reflect a cramped container limit, a tool bug, or a genuinely unroutable netlist. Preserving those distinctions across automated retries motivates the tool interfaces and run management developed in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces; once a run completes cleanly, Stage 4 (Evaluate) asks what the returned measurements actually establish about the design.

### Stage 4: Evaluating Candidates

Once implementation confirms what ran, evaluation checks whether the returned measurements actually answer the planned question, since clean execution alone does not establish measurement validity. A loop that relies on fast surrogates and cycle-level simulators to afford many evaluations can produce false positives when wiring delay dominates; establishing the NPU candidate's physical and functional feasibility requires checks appropriate to its implementation, including static timing analysis (STA),[^fn-sta-c03] design rule check (DRC), logic equivalence checking (LEC), CDC checks, and dynamic $IR$-drop analysis, and any study that has not reached those checks must keep its conclusions within the models evaluated.

Suppose a candidate with a wider centralized crossbar compiles cleanly and a C++ cycle simulator predicts higher accumulator throughput at the target clock frequency. If STA then reports a setup timing violation on the accumulator paths, while power-integrity analysis reports dynamic voltage drop ($IR$-drop) near critical buffers,[^fn-ir-drop-c03] evaluation records that timing fails the declared constraint. The throughput prediction assumes a frequency that this physical implementation cannot sustain, so the candidate cannot be accepted as an improvement.

[^fn-sta-c03]: **Static timing analysis (STA)**: An exhaustive verification method that calculates signal propagation delays across all circuit paths against clock constraints without dynamic simulation vectors. A setup timing violation indicates negative slack, meaning data arrives too late relative to the clock edge and the circuit cannot reliably operate at the target clock frequency.

[^fn-ir-drop-c03]: **IR drop**: A voltage decrease caused by current flowing through resistance in the power-distribution network. Reduced supply voltage can slow switching and contribute to timing violations.

Evaluation records each requirement separately as passed, failed, or unresolved, so a passing functional check does not cancel the timing failure and a missing power estimate remains unknown. While the voltage-drop observation offers a clue to why timing failed, evaluation only registers the constraint violation; establishing its cause is the question for Interpret.

### Stage 5: Interpreting Empirical Results

Evaluation establishes which requirements hold under the tested conditions. Both gains and failures still need interpretation, because the same measured change can arise from different mechanisms. Stage 5 asks which explanation the evidence supports and what observation would distinguish the remaining possibilities.

For the NPU, the architect must distinguish a long crossbar path from inadequate power delivery, suboptimal cell sizing, or an incorrectly configured analysis. If we map this diagnosis onto the three operational layers, we can see where each workflow's repair loop can reach and where it must hand the problem back to people.

In a Layer 1 workflow, the model can help inspect a supplied timing report or regenerate an arithmetic expression inside one module. Access to a floorplan or clock-tree report can inform that isolated task without giving the model authority to coordinate a structural repair. The engineer evaluates the diagnosis, chooses the change, and carries it through integration and verification.

In a Layer 2 workflow, the repair loop runs automatically, adjusting parameters $\theta$ within the immutable container $\Theta$. A timing deficit may prompt local transformations such as gate sizing, swapping to lower-threshold-voltage ($V_t$) cells, buffer insertion, or useful clock skew tuning, which a Layer 2 optimizer can automate when those changes are permitted. In leading-edge FinFET and nanosheet nodes (such as 3\ nm), however, aggressive $V_t$ swapping raises subthreshold leakage exponentially ($I_{\text{sub}} \propto e^{-qV_t / (n k T)}$, with $n$ the subthreshold slope factor), which can consume the block's share of the prospective 3\ W envelope. When the attempted repairs fail to recover timing margin within the leakage limit because the failing paths cross the centralized crossbar, the next step is to inspect those paths and test whether interconnect delay explains the shortfall. If that diagnosis supports a crossbar repair that changes a frozen bus contract or memory organization, the optimizer must request architectural review to reopen Formulate.

In a Layer 3 workflow, the repair loop would be allowed to cross life-cycle and abstraction boundaries. If physical signoff reports that net delay dominates cell delay across the centralized crossbar, such a system would not be limited to relaxing the clock target or accepting the failure. It could carry that result back to Stage 2 (Explore) to propose distributed accumulator banks, to Stage 3 (Implement) to develop local reduction trees with a matching compiler schedule, and then to physical signoff again. Whether the revised design closes timing is a question for that new evaluation, not something the permission to redesign guarantees.

An automated system can assist this interpretation by extracting critical timing paths, comparing cell-delay versus net-delay ratios, and proposing explanatory hypotheses.[^fn-credit-assignment-c03] Isolating the contribution of wire delay requires running a controlled counterfactual through Implement and Evaluate, such as testing a shorter interconnect path or localized retiming under identical analysis settings while checking whether accompanying shifts in buffering, placement, or capacitive load confound the result; that diagnostic work needs its own run budget so counterfactual experiments cannot consume the study's overall allocation.

If the evidence supports long shared global interconnect as the limiting factor, the next iteration can test the distributed-bank alternative, whether a Layer 3 system or an architect proposes it. That iteration develops the new design's local reduction paths, control logic, and software schedule, then checks timing, power, and numerical behavior again under physical signoff. Deciding which observations justify structural redesign, and which explanations still need testing, connects this stage to the verification and feedback methods developed in @sec-feedback-verification-trust.

[^fn-credit-assignment-c03]: **The architectural credit assignment problem**: In multi-stage closed-loop design, attributing a downstream physical failure (such as negative slack, routing congestion, or localized $IR$-drop) to an upstream design decision is a classic credit assignment challenge. A timing violation could originate from an over-aggressive clock constraint in Formulate, a poor microarchitectural topology in Explore, awkward coding style in Implement, or suboptimal seed initialization in physical synthesis. Sensitivity analysis and controlled counterfactual trials can help distinguish these causes before triggering expensive structural redesigns.

Because a plausible generated explanation remains a hypothesis until observations can distinguish it from competing causes, automating this diagnosis is a capability to demonstrate within the study's scope. When the available runs cannot isolate a single cause, the study retains the competing explanations and either requests further investigation or stops for review, treating a clearer account of what remains unknown as a useful outcome alongside a supported design recommendation.

### Stage 6: Reviewing Evidence and Committing Decisions

Commit brings the study to a reviewed decision on what the completed work justifies doing next: advancing a candidate, rejecting it, revising the question, or stopping with unresolved issues. Because the consequence depends on the study's scope, advancing a revised NPU block to subsystem integration carries different obligations from approving a full design for mask freeze.[^fn-mask-freeze-c03] When a revised NPU block satisfies its declared checks, the responsible architect reviews the tested design and software revisions, the comparison conditions, the explanation for the improvement, and the remaining system-level limitations before recommending integration; if timing still fails, the architect can choose further work or close the study without selecting a candidate.

[^fn-mask-freeze-c03]: **Mask freeze**: The final signoff milestone (often termed tapeout) where physical layout geometries are locked and released to manufacture optical lithography reticles (photomasks). Unlike a software patch, a silicon defect found after mask freeze generally requires new masks and a respin, which at advanced process nodes is among the most expensive and time-consuming corrections a program can make.

Allowing routine iterations to proceed automatically within the scope and budget established during Formulate lets automation do useful work without making each tool invocation a separate approval, while reserving human review for when the planned decision is reached, the scope must change, or the stopping conditions call for it. When a study halts because it exhausted its run budget, that outcome ends the permitted work rather than establishing that no feasible design exists.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="From the NPU block to the Lighthouse subsystem"}
**Context.** The accumulator study examines one block in a candidate Lighthouse design. Its results must eventually be evaluated in the XR workload that motivated the design.

**Application.** Faster accumulation may shorten a workload stage, but additional transfers or memory contention may erase that gain. The integrated comparison must check workload deadlines, the matching software schedule, and power across the subsystem, including memory and leakage.

**Outcome.** A successful block study could justify evaluating the revised NPU in the surrounding system. Whether that Lighthouse candidate meets its 3\ W target and real-time requirements remains a question for the subsystem study.
:::

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Stop when the tools cannot observe the target"}
**The principle:** A valid architectural outcome includes rejecting every candidate, retaining the baseline reference, or halting exploration before tool dispatch when available tools cannot observe target physical reality.

**The application:** An analytical memory model such as CACTI derives its estimates from generic technology parameters, not from a leading-edge foundry's qualified bitcells, multi-threshold leakage distributions, or write-assist circuits, so at a node such as TSMC N3E its numbers are uncalibrated estimates rather than signoff-grade results. When evaluation prerequisites or calibrated tool collateral are missing, an AI-native design system should stop before dispatch, or label the returns as uncalibrated, rather than treat them as measurements. Stopping there is a valid outcome of the study, and its record should state what was missing.
:::

The six stages can now serve as a reference for planning a study. Their inputs, outputs, and reasons to revisit earlier work differ, even when one person or tool performs several activities (@tbl-stage-seams).

| **Stage** | **Starts from** | **Produces** | **Reason to revisit** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Formulate** | Product goals and system requirements. | A question, baseline, scope, checks, and stopping conditions. | Evidence calls the target, assumptions, or permitted changes into question. |
| **Explore** | The plan and what earlier candidates taught. | Candidate organizations or configurations, with reasons for testing them. | A candidate fails, or a result suggests a better alternative. |
| **Implement** | A candidate and the checks it needs. | Testable hardware and software, tool inputs, and execution results. | Artifacts need revision, or the intended checks did not run. |
| **Evaluate** | Execution results and the planned comparison. | Valid comparisons and passed, failed, or unresolved checks. | Conditions are mismatched or observations are insufficient. |
| **Interpret** | Checked results and possible explanations. | Supported explanations, remaining hypotheses, and proposed investigations. | Causes remain uncertain or another result contradicts the explanation. |
| **Commit** | The plan, comparisons, explanations, and limitations. | A reviewed decision to advance, reject, revise, or stop. | Missing evidence or a changed requirement reopens the decision. |
: **Each stage contributes something different to a design decision.** The reference distinguishes what an activity needs, what it contributes, and why it may be revisited. A single failure can require work in several stages. {#tbl-stage-seams tbl-colwidths="[15,25,30,30]"}

Evaluate needs both the results from Implement and the criteria declared in Formulate; Commit needs the accumulated work, not only the last interpretation.

The same seams mark how far a workflow's repair can reach when a check fails, as the NPU diagnosis showed. When even structural redesign cannot meet the goals, the repair routes back to Formulate for review of the targets, or the study stops without a candidate.

Preserving these connections in structured records lets another architect follow what happened, which layer governed the search, and why a specific repair was chosen.

## Design-Loop Cards and Documentation {#sec-design-loop-card}

Reviewing the NPU study requires more than its best timing report. Another architect needs to know which candidate produced it, which workload and constraints were used, why that candidate was selected, and what earlier failures taught the team. Much of this information may already exist in repositories, experiment logs, and verification reports. The documentation task is to connect it to the question and the resulting decision.

A *study record* provides this connected account by linking the plan, candidate revisions, comparisons, explanations, and failed or unfinished work to the final decision or stopping reason, whereas an *execution record* supplies the details of a single attempt, including its inputs, random seeds when applicable, library versions, tool environment, diagnostic outputs, and completion status. In the NPU example, one execution record registers a setup timing violation, while the study record explains how that observation led the team to test a banked accumulator design. Preserving both levels requires retaining each failed attempt and recording what changed on a retry, rather than overwriting a shared scratch directory and losing the information needed to explain an earlier result.

> **Design-loop card.** A short structured index, fixed before any tool runs, that records a scoped study's baseline, candidate space, execution budget, verification criteria, and reviewer, and links each later execution record back to that plan [@MitchellEtAl2019ModelCards; @GebruEtAl2021Datasheets]. It borrows contextual documentation from Model Cards and Datasheets for Datasets and points into existing engineering records rather than replacing them.

Keeping the study question between the product goal and individual tool runs helps a reviewer trace how a local result bears on a larger architectural commitment (@fig-structured-layer-above-rtl). This three-tier hierarchy organizes information dependencies rather than imposing a rigid software framework.

![**Scoped studies connect system goals to implementation results.** An explicit intermediate layer positions the architecture question, constraints, and linked artifacts between high-level system intent and low-level execution tools (simulators, compilers, and electronic design automation (EDA) engines). This structured binding preserves provenance from raw tool returns to reviewed architectural commitments.](images/fig-structured-layer-above-rtl){#fig-structured-layer-above-rtl width="72%" fig-alt="Diagram in which system intent and human judgment appear above a scoped architecture study, which links its question and artifacts to results from implementation tools below. Feedback connects the study to further design work and review."}

A raw cycle count, for example, tells a reviewer nothing without the workload trace that drove it and the simulator configuration. Similarly, a physical timing estimate requires the applicable PVT corners,[^fn-pvt-c03] calibrated library models, and explicit timing constraints specified in Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) files.[^fn-sdc-c03] Linking each tool return to the study question lets a reviewer distinguish a simulated cycle improvement from a design that passes DRC and STA signoff, and shows which comparisons must rerun when an upstream assumption changes.

[^fn-pvt-c03]: **Process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners**: Combinations of device-model and operating assumptions used to check a design under different conditions. The limiting combination can differ across timing and power checks.

[^fn-sdc-c03]: **Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC)**: A format for specifying clocks, input and output delays, timing exceptions, and related constraints used by synthesis and timing-analysis tools.

Within the same Lighthouse design, a separate study could compare 2, 3, and 4\ MiB Level-2 (L2) cache capacities while holding the other architecture choices fixed. The question is whether fewer capacity misses reduce frame-time tail latency on the selected XRBench workload while meeting power, area, and access-time constraints. Power estimates must include leakage within the subsystem's 3\ W envelope. This memory comparison complements the accumulator study; each examines a different part of the system.

The cache example sits inside the kind of frozen container that Layer 2 optimization searches, where bus widths, cache line sizes, replacement policies, and interconnect protocols remain fixed, but with only three candidates it needs no learned optimizer and runs no design loop; it is a predetermined comparison. It still uses a design-loop card to record the baseline, candidates, physical checks, and commitment criteria before dispatch, governing a bounded parameter sweep before tackling unconstrained generated alternatives.

A cycle-level simulator would estimate frame times, while a static random-access memory (SRAM) model[^fn-sram-model-c03] would estimate the arrays' area, power, and access time. Checking the subsystem envelope also requires the other components' power contributions. Each tool therefore supplies part of the comparison, and the card links those parts to the same candidate and workload.

[^fn-sram-model-c03]: **SRAM memory models**: Dense multi-megabyte cache arrays use custom analog-digital bitcells and sense amplifiers that cannot be efficiently synthesized from standard logic gates. Architectural exploration relies on analytical tools (such as CACTI) or foundry memory compilers to evaluate area, access latency, dynamic read and write energy, and static leakage for specific banking configurations.

A machine-readable design-loop card gives automated optimization and human reviewers the same assumptions before any tool runs (@fig-filled-design-loop-card). It fixes the baseline, candidate space, execution budget, and evaluation criteria in a versioned file, and its result fields stay empty until executed checks return results.

![**A design-loop card separates planned work from results and decisions.** Structured schema for the prospective Lighthouse Level-2 (L2) cache comparison. The budget allows four cycle-level attempts and one SRAM screening evaluation per capacity. These limits and the verification checks bind upfront intent before dispatch, while evidence fields and commitment decisions remain open until executed checks return results.](images/fig-filled-design-loop-card){#fig-filled-design-loop-card width="75%" fig-alt="Illustration of a study card for a prospective XR cache study. A hypothesis precedes entries for the baseline, candidates, checks, execution budget, evidence needed, and responsible reviewer. No completed result is reported."}

The cycle-level budget allocates one trial for each capacity candidate (2, 3, and 4\ MiB) with room for exactly one rerun, in addition to the three SRAM screening evaluations. The ceiling is deliberately tight, because cycle-accurate simulation over extended workloads is expensive. If an execution aborts on a tool timeout, or if sampling of workload inputs leaves the 99th-percentile frame time too variable to separate the candidates within four cycle-level attempts, the architect stops and records the outcome as unresolved, as the card's budget requires. Although the accumulator and cache studies address the same prospective subsystem, their modular cards keep their failure domains separate. Adopting an altered NPU accumulator changes interconnect traffic and thermal dissipation, requiring the architect to revisit the cache card with updated background power assumptions.

Between them, the accumulator and cache studies show why an architect has to evaluate architectural choices and representation limits together. Just as a Layer 2 representation that permits only buffer-capacity changes cannot express a distributed accumulator organization even when a generator proposes one, sweeping cache capacity inside a fixed container will plateau once memory-bandwidth saturation throttles the frame rate. Relieving that bottleneck requires changes the container excludes, such as interconnect compression, altered network packet formats, or new compiler data layouts, and therefore demands a reformulated study whether an architect carries it out or a Layer 3 system someday proposes it under physical signoff feedback.

The following chapters develop these connections. @sec-data-representations-world-models examines what design and workload information methods need to use; @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization asks which methods can help answer a particular architecture question at acceptable cost. Reliable execution of the chosen checks is developed in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, and the interpretation and use of their results in @sec-feedback-verification-trust. These ingredients serve several stages rather than matching the stages one for one. Later chapters ask which conclusions transfer when the workload, tools, or decision change (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack), how to evaluate the complete system against alternatives (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect), and who owns the commitment (@sec-what-architect-owns). The companion laboratories offer small executable exercises for parts of this life cycle.

## Open Questions

Organizing design work into six explicit stages clarifies what each handoff must preserve, while exposing four open research problems in multi-stage pruning, causal diagnosis, container reformulation, and multi-study coordination:

- **How can tiered screening pipelines prune infeasible candidates early without discarding hardware topologies whose value requires co-adapted software and physical layout?** Screening candidates sequentially through behavioral simulation, logic synthesis, and place-and-route saves scarce EDA licenses, but strict early filters can reject a distributed accumulator topology simply because it was evaluated under a compiler schedule tuned for a centralized crossbar, much as rigid early docking filters in computational drug discovery discard novel molecular structures whose binding affinity emerges only after conformational relaxation. Conversely, compiling custom schedules and running physical placement for every candidate organization exhausts the study's evaluation budget on designs that violate basic functional or area constraints. Formulating multi-stage pruning policies with provable false-rejection bounds across coupled compiler and physical-design stages remains an open problem.

- **How can an automated workflow perform causal credit assignment when a post-route signoff check fails?** When static timing analysis or dynamic $IR$-drop signoff fails in a 3\ nm flow, the violation arrives as a gate-level path through extracted interconnect parasitics that could stem from an over-aggressive clock target in Formulate, a centralized crossbar topology in Explore, unpipelined RTL in Implement, or placement seed noise. Rerunning full physical implementation to test every competing hypothesis quickly exhausts the diagnostic budget, whereas misattributing wire-dominated delay to local cell sizing traps a Layer 2 optimizer in unproductive threshold-voltage ($V_t$) swaps. Designing counterfactual intervention policies that isolate the responsible upstream stage in the minimum number of tool executions is a foundational challenge for closed-loop repair.

- **What formal or empirical certificates distinguish an exhausted search budget from a physically infeasible problem formulation?** When a Layer 2 optimizer repeatedly fails to close timing on the NPU accumulator without exceeding the 3\ W subthreshold leakage budget, the failed runs alone do not prove that the frozen structural container $\Theta$ contains no viable parameter setting $\theta$. Continuing to sample inside an infeasible container wastes compute, whereas reopening Formulate prematurely to relax clock targets or alter bus contracts can mask a weak search algorithm. Combining physical scaling bounds, surrogate uncertainty calibration, and dual infeasibility certificates to determine when a design space is structurally exhausted would provide a principled trigger for escalating from parameter tuning to architectural reformulation.

- **How can modular block studies coordinate shared power, thermal, and bandwidth budgets without collapsing into a monolithic full-SoC search?** Decomposing a system into scoped design-loop cards keeps failure domains inspectable, yet committing a faster banked NPU accumulator alters bursty interconnect traffic and background thermal dissipation in ways that can invalidate a sibling Level-2 (L2) cache study within the same 3\ W envelope. Re-evaluating the entire subsystem at cycle-accurate and post-route fidelity after every block-level revision is computationally intractable, while static power and bandwidth allocations leave cross-block optimizations on the table. Drawing on how aerospace multidisciplinary design optimization coordinates airframe, propulsion, and control loops without a single monolithic solver, hardware workflows need sensitivity-aware interface contracts or bilevel coordination protocols that propagate local margin shifts across sibling studies and identify when coupled blocks must be solved jointly.

## Summary

The life cycle connects an architecture question to candidate generation, implementation, comparison, interpretation, and a reviewed decision. In the NPU example, a promising throughput prediction led to physical checks, a timing failure, and investigation of another accumulator organization. Progress came from connecting what each activity learned to what the next one needed. The sequence can repeat, overlap, or return to the original question as the study develops.

This organization gives the rest of the book a common framework while leaving its practical implementation open. A small cache comparison may use direct enumeration; a broader AI-native study may generate and develop different hardware–software organizations. Both need meaningful comparisons and an account of what the results justify. The amount of automation can change without removing those engineering needs.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Begin with a testable question.** The baseline, requirements, permitted changes, and stopping conditions make later comparisons meaningful while leaving room for alternative organizations.
- **Connect generation to implementation.** A proposed organization needs a representation that can express it, along with matching hardware, software, and checks before its benefits can be assessed.
- **Separate evaluation from interpretation.** Establish what passed, failed, or remains unknown, then investigate why and use the findings to guide another design.
- **Revisit the work affected by a result.** Preserve earlier results whose assumptions still hold, and investigate coupled causes before selecting a repair.
- **Keep the decision proportional to the evidence.** Retain the conditions, attempts, and limitations needed for review, since advancing, rejecting, revising, and stopping unresolved are all possible outcomes and exhausting a run budget only ends the permitted search rather than proving the target infeasible.
:::

To generate and compare the accumulator alternatives, a method needs descriptions that expose their different organizations while retaining the workload and constraints. @sec-data-representations-world-models examines how to represent that information, beginning with the architectural data from which those descriptions are built.
